cards.html:
You are halfway through a change when your lead asks you to check something on main. Your working directory is dirty and not ready to commit. git stash takes your uncommitted changes, saves them on a stack, and gives you a clean working directory.

terminal:

git stash push -m "half-done age validation"   # or just: git stash
git switch main                                  # do the urgent thing
git switch feature/age
git stash list

expected output:

stash@{0}: On feature/age: half-done age validation

CommandWhat it does
git stash show -p stash@{0}Show the diff of a stash.
git stash applyRe-apply the newest stash, keep it on the stack (safe: if it goes wrong, the stash is still there).
git stash popRe-apply and delete it from the stack (only if it applied without conflict).
git stash push -- src/app.pyStash only specific files.
git stash -uInclude untracked (new) files. Without -u, new files stay in your working directory.
git stash drop stash@{1}Delete one stash.
git stash branch fix-age stash@{0}Create a branch from the commit where you stashed and apply the stash there: the cleanest way out of a stash that conflicts.

Watch out: Stash conflicts

If the code changed since you stashed, apply/pop can conflict, exactly like a merge. Resolve the markers and git add the files. pop does not delete a stash that conflicted, so remove it yourself with git stash drop once you are sure. Stashes are local and easy to forget: treat them as hours-long parking, not storage.

This is what a conflicting pop really looks like. Note the last line:

expected output:

$ git stash pop
Auto-merging notes.txt
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in notes.txt
...
The stash entry is kept in case you need it again.

SituationRecipe
Run the tests on only what you staged, to check the commit you are about to makegit stash push --keep-index -u, run uv run pytest, then git stash pop. The unstaged and untracked rest is parked meanwhile.
Park only the staged partgit stash push --staged
You started work on main by mistakegit stash, git switch -c feat/x, git stash pop. (Simpler: git switch -c feat/x carries uncommitted changes along, no stash needed.)
Pull, but you have local editsgit pull --rebase --autostash (or the rebase.autoStash setting from Section 2.2).
Take one file out of a stashgit restore --source=stash@{0} -- path/to/file

What if… I dropped a stash I still needed?

What happens: git stash drop printed Dropped refs/stash@{0} (a861edc…), and git stash list no longer shows it. Stashes have no reflog entry after they are dropped.

What you do: A stash is stored as a commit, and Git does not delete unreachable commits immediately (garbage collection keeps them for weeks). If the drop message is still on your screen, git stash apply a861edc brings it back. Otherwise, search for dangling commits. This worked in our lab:

$ git fsck --no-reflogs --unreachable | grep commit
unreachable commit a861edc17c894ada149afd5003dd19e0ae61a699
$ git log --oneline --no-walk a861edc
a861edc On main: precious work
$ git stash apply a861edc

Stash commits are easy to spot: their message starts with On <branch>: or WIP on <branch>:.

cards.s: `git worktree`: two branches checked out at once
cards.html:
Stashing is fine for five minutes. But suppose a colleague asks you to review PR 42, which needs a 10-minute test run, while you are in the middle of a big refactor. Switching branches would disturb your editor, your virtual environment and your uncommitted files. A worktree is a second working directory attached to the same repository: same history and objects, different checked-out branch.

terminal:

git worktree add ../credit-api-pr42 feature/new-endpoint
cd ../credit-api-pr42 && uv sync && uv run pytest   # review here
cd ../credit-api                                    # your work: untouched
git worktree list
git worktree remove ../credit-api-pr42              # when done

expected output:

cards.s: `git worktree`: two branches checked out at once
cards.html:
/home/you/credit-api        3f2a1c0 [feature/refactor]
/home/you/credit-api-pr42   7c19e2b [feature/new-endpoint]

Use git worktree add -b hotfix/crash ../hotfix origin/main to create a new branch for an urgent fix in its own folder. Two rules: a branch can be checked out in only one worktree at a time, and if you delete a worktree folder by hand, run git worktree prune.

What if… I try to check out the same branch in two worktrees?

What happens: Real output:

$ git worktree add ../credit-api-wt main
fatal: 'main' is already used by worktree at '/home/you/credit-api'

cards.s: `git worktree`: two branches checked out at once
cards.html:
Why: If two folders had the same branch checked out, a commit in one would silently change the branch under the other's feet.

What you do: Check out a detached copy for reading and testing (git worktree add --detach ../wt main), or create a new branch from it (-b review/main ../wt main).

What if… my ML training run takes two hours and I want to keep coding?

cards.s: `git worktree`: two branches checked out at once
cards.html:
What you do: This is where worktrees shine for ML work. git worktree add ../credit-api-train exp/new-features, then cd there, uv sync, and start the training. It reads that folder's code, so you can edit, switch branches and run tests in your main folder without changing the code under a running job. Each worktree needs its own virtual environment (uv sync creates .venv per folder; uv's global cache makes this fast). Large data files are not shared automatically: point both at one data directory through a config value or environment variable instead of copying gigabytes.

Interview tip

cards.s: `git worktree`: two branches checked out at once
cards.html: "For quick context switches I use stash; when I need to run a PR's test suite or a hotfix in parallel with my own work, I use git worktree, so both have their own working directory and environment."
Git rarely loses committed work. The trick is knowing where to look. The tools below cover 95 % of "help, I broke it" situations.

git reset <commit> moves your branch pointer back to <commit>. The mode decides what happens to the changes in between (Figure 8): --soft keeps them staged (handy to redo the last commit: git reset --soft HEAD~1), --mixed (the default) keeps them as unstaged edits, --hard throws them away. Only use reset on commits you have not pushed to a shared branch.

git revert <commit> creates a new commit that undoes an old one. History is not rewritten, so this is the safe way to undo something on main that is already pushed or deployed. To revert a merge commit, tell Git which parent is the mainline: git revert -m 1 <merge-sha>.

What if… I revert a merged feature, fix it, and merge it again?

What happens: Friday: feature/age was merged, broke production, and you reverted the merge with git revert -m 1. Monday: you add a fix commit to feature/age and merge again. In our lab, the merge stopped with a strange conflict, and the file age.py from the original feature was simply missing:

CONFLICT (modify/delete): api.py deleted in HEAD and modified in
feature/age.  Version feature/age of api.py left in tree.

In other cases there is no conflict at all, and only the new fix arrives, without the feature it fixes.

Why: The revert undid the changes, but the original commits are still in main's history. Git considers them already merged, so it only brings in commits made after the first merge.

What you do: First revert the revert, then merge. Git calls the result "Reapply":

git merge --abort
git revert <sha-of-the-revert-commit>   # 'Reapply "Merge branch ..."'
git merge feature/age                   # now brings only the fix

This worked cleanly in the lab. Remember the rule: a reverted merge is not "unmerged" in Git's eyes.

git reflog is Git's diary of where HEAD has been, including commits that no branch points to anymore. It is how you undo a bad reset --hard or a rebase that went wrong:

terminal:

git reflog

expected output:

e41c2d8 HEAD@{0}: rebase (finish): returning to refs/heads/feature
9a0d3b1 HEAD@{1}: rebase (pick): add test for age
a77e0b3 HEAD@{5}: commit: oops forgot file      <- before the rebase

terminal:

git branch rescue a77e0b3       # put a branch on the old state
# or move the current branch back: git reset --hard HEAD@{5}

git cherry-pick <sha> copies one commit onto your current branch. Typical use: a bug fix landed on main, and you need exactly that fix on a release branch. Add -x to record where it came from. A range works too (git cherry-pick A^..B copies A through B). If it conflicts, you resolve exactly as in a rebase, then git cherry-pick --continue (or --abort).

What if… Git says I am in "detached HEAD" state?

What happens: You checked out a commit or tag instead of a branch (git switch --detach v0.3.0, or git checkout 7c19e2b; git bisect does it too). Git prints HEAD is now at 0bf8e3c … and a long warning.

Why: Normally HEAD points to a branch, and the branch moves when you commit. Detached, HEAD points straight at a commit. You can look around and even commit, but no branch remembers those commits.

What you do: Just looking? git switch - (or git switch main) and nothing happened. Made commits you want to keep? git switch -c rescue before switching away. Already switched away? The commits are in git reflog. CI runners usually check out in detached HEAD too (they check out an exact SHA), which is why some tools inside CI cannot tell the branch name and read it from $GITHUB_REF_NAME instead.

SituationRecovery
…committed to main instead of a branch (not pushed)git branch feat/x (keep the commits on a new branch), then git reset --hard origin/main (move main back), then git switch feat/x.
…want to change the last commit's message or add a forgotten file (not pushed)git add forgotten.py && git commit --amend (--no-edit keeps the message).
…committed a file that should not be in the commitgit reset --soft HEAD~1, git restore --staged file, commit again.
…ran git reset --hard and lost commitsgit reflog, find the line before the reset, git reset --hard HEAD@{n}.
…ran git reset --hard and lost uncommitted editsUnstaged changes are gone: Git never saw them. Staged ones can be found with git fsck --lost-found (as blobs, without file names). Your editor's local history (VS Code: Timeline view) is the last hope. Commit early, even as "wip".

SituationRecovery
…deleted a branchgit branch -D prints the SHA: git branch name <sha>. Otherwise git reflog shows its last commit.
…pushed a broken commit to maingit revert <sha> and push. Never reset + force-push a shared branch.
…committed a secretRotate the secret first, then clean up (Level 2). Deleting the file in a new commit does not remove it from history.

Concept: How long does Git keep "lost" commits?

Reflog entries are kept for 90 days by default (gc.reflogExpire), but only 30 days for commits that no branch contains any more, such as the ones a reset --hard left behind (gc.reflogExpireUnreachable). Commits that are not even in the reflog, such as dropped stashes, survive at least 14 days (gc.pruneExpire) before git gc may delete them. So you have weeks, not minutes, but not forever. And the reflog is local: a fresh clone has no reflog of your work.

cards.sub: `git bisect`: which commit broke the test?
cards.html:
CI says test_predict_returns_probability fails on main, but it passed at release v0.3.0 fifty commits ago. Bisect does a binary search over those commits: about six test runs instead of fifty.

terminal:

git bisect start
git bisect bad                    # current commit is broken
git bisect good v0.3.0            # this tag was fine
git bisect run uv run pytest tests/test_api.py -q
# ... Git checks out commits and runs the test for you ...
git bisect reset                  # back to where you started

expected output:

7c19e2b5 is the first bad commit
    refactor: rename probability field

cards.sub: `git bisect`: which commit broke the test?
cards.html: git bisect run treats exit code 0 as good and 1–127 (except 125) as bad, which is exactly how pytest reports. This is one more reason why every commit on main should pass CI: bisect only works if the history is made of testable states.

Tests are not the only thing you can bisect. Suppose the nightly evaluation shows ROC-AUC fell from 0.79 to 0.74 sometime since v0.3.0, and every unit test is green. Write a small script whose exit code answers "is this commit good?". Exit code 125 tells bisect "this commit cannot be tested, skip it", for example a commit where the code does not even build:

bisect_auc.sh:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# exit 0 = good, 1 = bad, 125 = cannot test (skip)
uv sync --locked -q || exit 125
uv run python -m credit_api.train > /dev/null || exit 125
python3 -c "import json, sys
auc = json.load(open('metrics/metrics.json'))['roc_auc']
sys.exit(0 if auc >= 0.77 else 1)"

We ran a simulated version of this over nine commits, one of them a broken build. Shortened output:

expected output:

$ git bisect start HEAD v0.3.0
$ git bisect run ./bisect_auc.sh
[7392b8c] wip: broken build           <- exit 125: skipped
running './bisect_auc.sh'
Bisecting: 1 revision left to test after this (roughly 1 step)
[e09679c] fix: build
running './bisect_auc.sh'
589218d37b72df27e553f88a026aba7e07f9c6f7 is the first bad commit
    refactor: change encoding
bisect found first bad commit
$ git bisect reset

Three things make this work in practice: training must be deterministic (fixed seed, fixed split), the threshold must sit clearly between the good and bad values (0.77 between 0.79 and 0.74, not 0.789), and the script must run from a copy outside the repository (bisect checks out old commits, which might not contain your script). Copy it to /tmp first.

What if… the bug only appears with data that changed, not code?

Then bisect over commits finds nothing, because every commit is good with the old data and bad with the new. Bisect needs one variable. Pin the data (a DVC version or a dated snapshot, Level 4) and bisect the code, or keep the code fixed and compare the data versions instead.
